claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by enhanced dislocation-interface interactions.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order mediate the dislocation-interface interactions.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order increase the initial resistance to dislocation motion.
Dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC interfaces create excessive local stress concentrations.
Excessive local stress concentrations produced by interfacial dislocation pile-ups cause rapid acceleration of creep.
The starting nanoscale FCC/BCC multilayer has inherent severe lattice distortion and pre-existing short-range order.
Controlled changes in alloy composition can systematically vary lattice distortion between the layers.
Lattice-parameter mismatch induced by severe lattice distortion and short-range order produces interfacial dislocation pile-ups and localized stress concentrations.
Increasing lattice distortion raises resistance to dislocation motion specifically at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Greater interfacial resistance causes dislocations to accumulate and interact more strongly.
Accumulated localized stress triggers accelerated creep after a critical threshold is crossed.
Higher-distortion multilayers will initially creep more slowly because dislocations are pinned more effectively.
A marked increase in creep rate will occur when critical interfacial dislocation density and stress are reached.
Higher-distortion samples will exhibit more interfacial stress concentration and dislocation blockage than reduced-distortion samples.
Reduced lattice distortion and less pronounced short-range order permit more uniform dislocation flow.
More uniform dislocation flow produces less localized stress accumulation and a steadier creep rate.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoscale multilayer architectures and a service-relevant range of temperatures and applied stresses.
The critical pile-up threshold and resulting creep acceleration may depend on subtle nanoscale compositional differences.
